message.content:
You are checking the novelty of two candidate simulation-study designs for a judgement-and-decision-making paper. For each, find the closest existing modelling papers and say whether the specific test has already been done.

CANDIDATE E. HOT-STOVE / SMALL-SAMPLE MODEL PREDICTING FEEDBACK EFFECTS PER PROBLEM (Denrell & March 2001 Org Sci 10.1287/orsc.12.5.523.10092; Denrell 2007 Psych Review 10.1037/0033-295x.114.1.177; Erev et al. 2017 Psych Review BEAST 10.1037/rev0000062). Question: has a minimal small-sample (natural-mean, k-sample) model with parameters fixed from one dataset been used to predict out-of-sample the problem-level shift between no-feedback and feedback blocks (as in CPC15/CPC18 choice-prediction data), or the description–experience (DE) gap in the Wulff, Mergenthaler-Canseco & Hertwig 2018 Psych Bull meta-analytic database (10.1037/bul0000115)? Note what BEAST and the CPC18 winners already do (Plonsky et al. 2019 "Predicting human decisions with behavioral theories and machine learning"; Erev et al. CPC18; Bourgin et al. 2019 "Cognitive model priors"; Peterson et al. 2021 Science choices13k), and whether small-sample models (e.g., Hertwig & Pleskac 2010; Fox & Hadar; Plonsky, Teodorescu & Erev 2015 "Reliance on small samples, the wavy recency effect"; Erev & Roth "sampling"; Wulff's "Sampling-based models" e.g., Wulff & van den Bos; Spektor & Wulff; Hills & Hertwig) have been fitted to the Wulff database or used to predict problem-level DE gaps.

CANDIDATE F. CONFIDENCE REGRESSION ARTEFACTS IN THE CONFIDENCE DATABASE (Rahnev et al. 2020 Nature Human Behaviour "The Confidence Database"; Erev, Wallsten & Budescu 1994 10.1037/0033-295x.101.3.519; Juslin, Winman & Olsson 2000 10.1037/0033-295x.107.2.384). Test: a zero-bias noisy-evidence (SDT with confidence noise) model predicts the hard–easy effect magnitude per dataset from fitted noise. Question: has the hard–easy effect / over-underconfidence been analysed across the Confidence Database, or predicted from noise parameters? Check works citing the Confidence Database mentioning hard-easy, overconfidence, calibration, and model comparisons across the database (e.g., Shekhar & Rahnev 2021/2024 "The nature of metacognitive inefficiency"/"lognormal meta noise"; Guggenmos 2022 "Reverse engineering of metacognition" eLife; Rausch/Hellmann et al. 2023 "confidence models"; Xue, Shekhar & Rahnev; Mamassian & de Gardelle CNC; Boundy-Singer; "Rahnev hard-easy").

TOOLS. A Python helper exists at /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_novelty_oa.py (do not edit it; if you need your own script name it /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_novelty_EF_*.py). Load keys first in every Bash call: `cd /tmp/jdmsim && set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a; python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py ...`. Commands:
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py cites <W-id>[,<W-id>...] "<search terms or empty>" [abs]` lists works citing any of the IDs (first 50), optional abstracts.
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py search "<terms>" [abs]` full-text search.
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py work <DOI> [<DOI>...]` prints OpenAlex id, year, DOI, title, abstract.
- `python3 scratch_novelty_oa.py ids <DOI>...` resolves OpenAlex IDs.
Known IDs: Denrell & March 2001 W2165357065; Denrell 2007 W2079843690; BEAST 2017 W2592002913; Wulff 2018 W2772751317; Erev Wallsten Budescu 1994 W2043763623; Juslin et al. 2000 W2145284651. Resolve the Confidence Database DOI via search ("The Confidence Database" Rahnev 2020) then `ids`.
For E: search works citing Wulff 2018 with terms like "model", "sampling", "predict", "small samples", "feedback"; works citing BEAST with "feedback", "small samples", "out-of-sample". For F: works citing the Confidence Database with "hard-easy", "overconfidence", "calibration", "noise", "model comparison"; works citing Erev 1994/Juslin 2000 with "Confidence Database". Use WebSearch (load with ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch"). Read abstracts of the closest hits; full text (WebFetch) only where needed. Do not download data files. Keep DOIs exactly as returned by OpenAlex/Crossref, never from memory.

Return (compact markdown, one section per candidate): (1) closest 3–6 modelling papers with DOI, year, one line on what they did; (2) verdict: NOVEL / PARTLY DONE (say what remains) / DONE; (3) confidence (low/medium/high) with one-line reason.

# About me

I am Lukas, a social psychologist, meta-scientist and open science advocate, who mostly uses you to get research done and build the tooling that supports it (in addition to teaching support). I have a solid understanding of software development and infrastructure, but am no expert, so that I will often need clear recommendations and explanations. Most of what I build is tooling for one-off projects, most is not intended to be production-ready or backwards-compatible. Feel free to clarify that project-by-project, but generally lean, efficient and clear code is more important than any backwards-compatible shim or edge-case handling.

I also regularly need your help in writing. For that, and in code, the most annoying failure mode is when history leaks in - when a text argues against its previous versions, or code comments are more about what is gone than about what the curent code does. Here, writing and reviewing outputs from the perspective of a new reader is essential.

# How to work

## Delegation: Fable as Orchestrator

When the session model is Fable, work **orchestrator-first**: plan, delegate substantive work to cheaper subagents, then review and synthesize. Fable itself keeps task decomposition, design decisions and judgment calls, reviewing subagent output, final synthesis and user-facing writing, plus edits so trivial that delegating would take longer. Everything else — implementation, broad searches, analyses, mechanical batch work — goes to subagents by default.

## Using sub-agents

- **Default subagent model: Opus** (`model: "opus"` on the Agent tool / workflow `agent()` calls). Drop to Sonnet or Haiku for clearly mechanical, high-volume steps; reserve Fable-model subagents for only the hardest verify/judge stages.
- **codex CLI** — via the `codex-delegate` skill: (a) independent second opinions and code review (read-only), and (b) self-contained implementation tasks with `--approve-for-me` — good for parallel, independent work streams.
- **agy CLI** (Antigravity; Gemini 3.x + others, `agy models` lists them) — via the `agy-delegate` skill: (a) **large-context reads** — digesting big files, PDFs, logs, or datasets that would bloat Claude context — and (b) **cross-model second opinions**.
- **In Workflow scripts**, reach codex/agy through cheap relay agents: `agent(relayPrompt, {model: 'sonnet', effort: 'low'})`, where `relayPrompt` says "You are a relay agent. Pass the following payload prompt through the `codex-delegate` [or `agy-delegate`] skill, wait for its answer, and return its answer verbatim as your final message; do not answer the payload yourself." followed by the payload, the working directory, and mode/model choices. The relay is pure transport — the skill holds the CLI recipe; keep payload prompts self-contained. Make sure the agents run the request in the foreground, with generous timeout as a subagent that backgrounds codex and waits on monitors/notifications often never gets resumed, stranding the finished answer on disk. If a codex-relay subagent goes quiet, don't wait for it — `ls` for the output file and read it directly.
- Delegation must not degrade quality: give subagents complete, self-contained prompts with all needed context and file paths, and verify load-bearing results yourself rather than trusting a subagent's summary.
- Assign clear ownership of every delegated write target. When two or more agents or processes may write the same file, branch, key, or state object at the same time, give each an independent write target. Different fields in one state file are still one shared target. Merge outputs only when reading or reporting them. If one shared target is required, use one writer, a lock, or sequential phases.   replacement — heredoc rewrites hide the diff.

  `http://localhost:<port>/<file>`.

  live IDs after any tab error. Don't make navigate the first action of a
  browser_batch — create the tab first.

  screenshot to see the state instead of reissuing the identical call. Never put
  `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(…))` inside injected JS — the CDP call itself
  then times out.

contaminate stdout. Write to a file first (`gws … --format json > out.json 2>err.log`),

`--params '<JSON>'`, not as flags or positionals. After parsing any API response,
print the top-level keys before indexing into them.

When the same correction or unexpected failure recurs, encode the fix in a mechanism: a test, hook, lint rule, validation step, safer code default, or automation. Apply the mechanism now and remove the duplicate prose.

Keep a prose rule only when it requires judgment. State the decision and the failure mode it prevents.

## Statistical analyses

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. Do NOT introduce deviations (different year ranges, team/group-size filters, measures, controls, transformations) for convenience, tractability, or unstated preference. When a deviation is kept, state it and its justification plainly in the writeup and flag it briefly in the code.

## Status Reports and Summaries: Plain Over Clever

When reporting progress, findings, or decisions, write like a technical changelog,
not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use
ASD-STE100, but deviate where that increases clarity and readability.

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3
   startup; hashing 300 MB takes 0.10 s" — not "The manifest binding is in,
   positioned with the other startup refusals, and the agent measured the cost
   rather than assuming it."
2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and
   its one-line reason; drop the story of how it was reached unless asked.
3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items
   (fixes applied, decisions pending, open questions) go in a list or short table
   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.
6. **Ban editorializing connectors**: "which is the entire point", "worth noting
   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.
7. **Separate done / pending / needs-my-decision** into visibly distinct blocks,
   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

```html

```

- Escape `#` as `%23`; keep double quotes outside, single quotes inside.

## Keys

Reusable API keys live in `~/.claude/api_keys.env` (private to this machine, never shared). Load them with `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a` before running a script that needs them. 

Holds OpenAlex keys: `OPENALEX_API_KEY` (default) and `OPENALEX_API_KEYS` (comma-separated list of all keys). Rotate when quota is exhausted.

## Model Versions

Never assume that a model version I specify does not exist just because it's newer than your training data. If you're uncertain whether a model exists, search the web to verify. Never silently substitute an older version.

## API Cost Management

CRITICAL: Before launching any substantial paid-API job (batch LLM calls, large embedding/generation runs, anything looping over many items), explicitly estimate and confirm the cost with me *before* spending:
1. **State the estimate up front**: (price per token × tokens/call × number of calls), and say it out loud before running. Get confirmation for anything beyond a few dollars.
2. **Watch reasoning/thinking models**: a thinking model bills its hidden reasoning tokens as output and can cost ~10-30× a plain model for the same task. Prefer non-thinking models when output is short (e.g. a small JSON), and cap/lower the reasoning budget when a thinking model is needed.
3. **Use the cheapest viable provider/routing**: on OpenRouter pin cheapest-provider routing WITH a performance floor — `provider: {sort: "price", preferred_min_throughput: 40}` (tok/s; `preferred_max_latency` also exists) — because a pure price sort can route to a host queuing requests for minutes each. Add `require_parameters: true` when the call needs structured output (the cheapest host for a model does not always support it). Enable prompt caching when a large prefix is reused. Use `flex` tiers with OpenAi and Gemini that offer batch pricing at the cost of higher latency.
4. **Capture actual spend**: request usage/cost in the response and report it, so estimates can be checked against reality. If a run is substantially more expensive than estimated, stop and re-confirm.

## Backward Compatibility and Tests

Only add backward-compatibility shims, fallbacks, or dual-format handling in production systems. During development, keep the code clean — delete the old format and move on. If unsure whether something needs backward compatibility, ask before adding it.

Ensure core functionality is covered by tests, but avoid slop and large sets of smoke tests. Less is more.

## Make Reruns Safe

For every command, lifecycle step, or processing loop that may be retried, restarted, or interrupted, design it to reach the correct end state after any number of runs. This includes file-writing scripts and batched external calls.

Check two cases: a second run after success, and a run after interruption at each step. If a prior run may have left partial or stale state, inspect it before continuing. Reuse completed work, repair incomplete outputs, and remove artifacts or locks only after confirming that they are stale.

When deciding whether work is complete, compare stable content or identifiers, not file count or creation order.

## Commands For Me To Run: Copy-Pasteable, Never Illustrative

Any command written for me to run should work as-is when pasted into my shell from the
project root. No placeholders I have to resolve, and no interpreter or tool that is
not on my PATH — I copy what you write and run it.

In practice this means naming the project's own interpreter or entry point rather than
a generic one: `.venv/bin/python -m extract.export --release abc123`, not
`python -m extract.export ...`.

## Verification Before Finishing

Always verify that changes work (run tests, render outputs, check results) before presenting them as complete. Don't leave the user with "to verify, do X" — do it yourself.

When modifying code that produces visual output (plots, charts, UI components), always render and visually inspect the result before presenting the change as complete. Never declare formatting fixes "done" based on code logic alone, except for internal-facing HTML pages. For these, trust your judgement.

When editing something that is deployed (e.g. a GH page), deploying it is part of the task. When the edit is trivial, deploy. When it needs my review, ask for confirmation - but never let me guess whether the latest update is live.

# Working with git

## Committing: Fetch Before Building a Commit Stack

`git fetch` and check `main...origin/main` BEFORE committing, especially when building a stack. 
Also check `git log` for local commits that appeared since the session started (a collaborator or another session may have committed from the same checkout); verify shared files weren't clobbered before stacking on top.

## Parallel Agents in Git Worktrees

- **Merge by the agent's merge-base, never against current main/master.** An agent branches from
  the state that existed when it started, so `git diff main <branch>` carries *deletions of
  everything merged since*; applying it silently reverts already-merged work, with nothing in the
  output to indicate it. Use
  `git diff $(git merge-base main <branch>) <branch> -- <file>` to get only the agent's own
  changes, and re-verify previously merged work after each merge — not just the piece just landed.
- **Remove each worktree as it lands, not at the end.** Each is a full checkout; a wide wave can
  fill the disk mid-session, and worktree creation then fails with "No space left on device".

  (`ls foo* 2>/dev/null || true`).

## Chrome Extension: Local Files, Tabs, Busy Pages

- The extension cannot open `file://` URLs. To view local HTML, serve the directory
  (`python3 -m http.server <port>`, backgrounded) and open
  `http://localhost:<port>/<file>`.
- Never reuse a tabId from an earlier turn or session; call tabs_context_mcp for
  live IDs after any tab error. Don't make navigate the first action of a
  browser_batch — create the tab first.
- If a screenshot/scroll/javascript call times out, the page is mid-load: take one
  screenshot to see the state instead of reissuing the identical call. Never put
  `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(…))` inside injected JS — the CDP call itself
  then times out.

## Google Workspace

For any Google Workspace task (Docs, Sheets, Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Slides, Forms), use the `gws` CLI (`/opt/homebrew/bin/gws`). Discover the API with `gws <service> --help` and `gws schema <service.resource.method>`. Fall back to browser automation only for things gws cannot do, such as viewing rendered output.

Never pipe `gws` output directly into a JSON parser: keyring warnings and preamble
contaminate stdout. Write to a file first (`gws … --format json > out.json 2>err.log`),
`head -c 300` it to confirm it is JSON, then parse. Pass API arguments through
`--params '<JSON>'`, not as flags or positionals. After parsing any API response,
print the top-level keys before indexing into them.

## Sanity-Check Prompts

If a user prompt seems unrelated to the current project/working directory, or references files, concepts, or protocols that don't exist in the codebase, ask the user to confirm before proceeding. They may be in the wrong folder.

## Scratch / Throwaway Files

Name temporary or throwaway files with a `scratch` prefix (e.g. `scratch.py`, `scratch_notes.md`, `scratch_test.js`). The `/wrap` end-of-session skill detects files matching `scratch*` and offers to commit or delete them during wrap-up.

## Recurring Corrections Become Mechanisms

When the same correction or unexpected failure recurs, encode the fix in a mechanism: a test, hook, lint rule, validation step, safer code default, or automation. Apply the mechanism now and remove the duplicate prose.

Use the strongest mechanism available. Prefer a restriction that makes an invalid state impossible. If that is not possible, use a lint or CI check, a shared helper, or a runtime check.

Keep a prose rule only when it requires judgment. State the decision and the failure mode it prevents.

## Statistical analyses

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

### Reproducing / Replicating Prior Analyses

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. Do NOT introduce deviations (different year ranges, team/group-size filters, measures, controls, transformations) for convenience, tractability, or unstated preference. If a deviation is genuinely warranted (e.g. to fix a confound, handle censoring, or reduce compute), STOP and flag it explicitly, explain why, and get agreement before building on it. When a deviation is kept, state it and its justification plainly in the writeup and flag it briefly in the code.

# Writing

## Status Reports and Summaries: Plain Over Clever

When reporting progress, findings, or decisions, write like a technical changelog,
not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use
ASD-STE100, but deviate where that increases clarity and readability.

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3
   startup; hashing 300 MB takes 0.10 s" — not "The manifest binding is in,
   positioned with the other startup refusals, and the agent measured the cost
   rather than assuming it."
2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and
   its one-line reason; drop the story of how it was reached unless asked.
3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items
   (fixes applied, decisions pending, open questions) go in a list or short table
   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.
6. **Ban editorializing connectors**: "which is the entire point", "worth noting
   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.
7. **Separate done / pending / needs-my-decision** into visibly distinct blocks,
   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

## Jargon: I Know the Concepts, Not the Vocabulary

I have a solid working understanding of programming and systems, but no formal CS
training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

## Style Guides

My written style guides live in `~/Documents/Coding/style_guides`:

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

Read the relevant guide before drafting, revising, or reviewing my prose in that register, and before proposing additions to it.

## Statistical Results in Quarto/Rmd Reports

CRITICAL: NEVER write interpretive prose about statistical results you haven't seen. Produce the numbers first, read the rendered output, then write the text. The full conventions are in the `quarto-reporting` skill. Load it when creating or editing `.qmd` or `.Rmd` files.

## Academic References and DOIs

CRITICAL: NEVER fabricate DOIs, citation metadata, or reference details from memory. DOIs, author lists, titles, page numbers, and volume/issue numbers are exact identifiers — getting them wrong is worse than omitting them.

When creating references:
1. **Always look up DOIs** via the Crossref API (`https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic={url_encoded_reference}`) or web search. Never guess a DOI.
2. **Verify each DOI resolves** by fetching `https://api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}` and checking the returned metadata matches.
3. If a DOI cannot be found, **omit the DOI field** rather than inventing one.
4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

## Reading Academic Articles from HTML

When reading an academic article from an HTML page, ensure the page has fully loaded before extracting or searching its text, and confirm you are actually looking at the full text rather than just the abstract/landing view. A search that comes back empty can mean the content hasn't rendered yet, not that it isn't there. Take a screenshot to see what is actually on the page, before concluding a section is missing or treating the abstract as the whole article.

## Key failure mode - insufficient editing / drift

### The text has no memory of its drafts

Readers see only the final text, never its revision history. They do not know what an earlier draft said, what was wrong with it, or why a claim was softened or dropped. All external writing must read as a clean, self-contained statement of the *current* message, not as a reply to a previous version. Watch for "history leakage": phrasing that only makes sense against a framing the reader never saw. Tells include "not simply X", "rather than Y", "this is not the wrong variable", "to be fair", "the honest limits are narrower", "less a reprieve than a reminder", "we no longer…", and defensive hedges that rebut objections raised only in our own discussion. State the positive claim directly — say what the thing IS and what genuinely limits it, not what it is not relative to a draft.

This applies with full force to durable reference text: CLAUDE.md rules, code comments, docs, commit messages, skill files. A rule states the current fact ("GNU coreutils is on PATH"), never the story of its own correction — no "installed Jul 2026", "exists now", "no longer missing", "fixed since", "never assume X is absent". Those phrasings only make sense to someone who held the old, wrong belief; every future reader starts from the rule itself. Before saving any rule or comment, reread it as a stranger: if it reads as a rebuttal, rewrite it as the fact.

### When we agree to restructure, actually restart

If you and I agree to write a *fresh* draft or a new outline rather than edit the existing one, write it fresh from the agreed outline. Do not silently carry over the previous version's spine, ordering, emphasis, or lead just because it's already there — that is how an obsolete framing survives a "rewrite." Carry over only the verified facts, numbers and sources; treat the prior draft's structure as superseded unless we explicitly decide to keep a part of it.

# HTML files as a common output

Whenever you write long plans, proposals or report, assume HTML output as a default. It is more readable than md. When you need detailed feedback, include */html-comments*.

Link identifiers wherever they resolve: DOIs as `https://doi.org/…`, arXiv IDs as `https://arxiv.org/abs/…`, repos, issues, dataset accessions. Cited constructs (a named statistic, rubric or method) get a short hover gloss (`<abbr title="…">`) and a References section at the end.

Every standalone HTML file gets an emoji favicon as a `data:` URI, right after `<title>`:

```html
<link rel="icon" href="data:image/svg+xml,<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' viewBox='0 0 100 100'><text y='.9em' font-size='90'>🦸</text></svg>">
```

- Pick for the page's **topic**, never its type (no 📋 for every plan, 📊 for every
  report) — several are open at once and must be distinguishable. Keep it stable
  across edits to a file.
- Escape `#` as `%23`; keep double quotes outside, single quotes inside.
- Safari ignores SVG favicons: for participant- or reviewer-facing pages use
  `type="image/png"` with a base64 PNG (`base64 -i icon.png | tr -d '\n'`).

To open a webpage for the user, use the Bash tool to run `open <url>`. Do not use Claude artefacts by default. Keep scratch files local, deploy single collaborative files to surge.sh, and use GH pages for project-related files that are supposed to be shared.

# Working with APIs

## Keys

Reusable API keys live in `~/.claude/api_keys.env` (private to this machine, never shared). Load them with `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a` before running a script that needs them. 

Holds OpenAlex keys: `OPENALEX_API_KEY` (default) and `OPENALEX_API_KEYS` (comma-separated list of all keys). Rotate when quota is exhausted.

## Model Versions

Never assume that a model version I specify does not exist just because it's newer than your training data. If you're uncertain whether a model exists, search the web to verify. Never silently substitute an older version.

## API Cost Management

CRITICAL: Before launching any substantial paid-API job (batch LLM calls, large embedding/generation runs, anything looping over many items), explicitly estimate and confirm the cost with me *before* spending:
1. **State the estimate up front**: (price per token × tokens/call × number of calls), and say it out loud before running. Get confirmation for anything beyond a few dollars.
2. **Watch reasoning/thinking models**: a thinking model bills its hidden reasoning tokens as output and can cost ~10-30× a plain model for the same task. Prefer non-thinking models when output is short (e.g. a small JSON), and cap/lower the reasoning budget when a thinking model is needed.
3. **Use the cheapest viable provider/routing**: on OpenRouter pin cheapest-provider routing WITH a performance floor — `provider: {sort: "price", preferred_min_throughput: 40}` (tok/s; `preferred_max_latency` also exists) — because a pure price sort can route to a host queuing requests for minutes each. Add `require_parameters: true` when the call needs structured output (the cheapest host for a model does not always support it). Enable prompt caching when a large prefix is reused. Use `flex` tiers with OpenAi and Gemini that offer batch pricing at the cost of higher latency.
4. **Capture actual spend**: request usage/cost in the response and report it, so estimates can be checked against reality. If a run is substantially more expensive than estimated, stop and re-confirm.

# Coding practices

## Backward Compatibility and Tests

Only add backward-compatibility shims, fallbacks, or dual-format handling in production systems. During development, keep the code clean — delete the old format and move on. If unsure whether something needs backward compatibility, ask before adding it.

Ensure core functionality is covered by tests, but avoid slop and large sets of smoke tests. Less is more.

## Make Reruns Safe

For every command, lifecycle step, or processing loop that may be retried, restarted, or interrupted, design it to reach the correct end state after any number of runs. This includes file-writing scripts and batched external calls.

Check two cases: a second run after success, and a run after interruption at each step. If a prior run may have left partial or stale state, inspect it before continuing. Reuse completed work, repair incomplete outputs, and remove artifacts or locks only after confirming that they are stale.

When deciding whether work is complete, compare stable content or identifiers, not file count or creation order.

## Commands For Me To Run: Copy-Pasteable, Never Illustrative

Any command written for me to run should work as-is when pasted into my shell from the
project root. No placeholders I have to resolve, and no interpreter or tool that is
not on my PATH — I copy what you write and run it.

In practice this means naming the project's own interpreter or entry point rather than
a generic one: `.venv/bin/python -m extract.export --release abc123`, not
`python -m extract.export ...`.

## Verification Before Finishing

Always verify that changes work (run tests, render outputs, check results) before presenting them as complete. Don't leave the user with "to verify, do X" — do it yourself.

When modifying code that produces visual output (plots, charts, UI components), always render and visually inspect the result before presenting the change as complete. Never declare formatting fixes "done" based on code logic alone, except for internal-facing HTML pages. For these, trust your judgement.

When editing something that is deployed (e.g. a GH page), deploying it is part of the task. When the edit is trivial, deploy. When it needs my review, ask for confirmation - but never let me guess whether the latest update is live.

# Working with git

## Committing: Fetch Before Building a Commit Stack

`git fetch` and check `main...origin/main` BEFORE committing, especially when building a stack. 
Also check `git log` for local commits that appeared since the session started (a collaborator or another session may have committed from the same checkout); verify shared files weren't clobbered before stacking on top.

## Parallel Agents in Git Worktrees

- **Merge by the agent's merge-base, never against current main/master.** An agent branches from
  the state that existed when it started, so `git diff main <branch>` carries *deletions of
  everything merged since*; applying it silently reverts already-merged work, with nothing in the
  output to indicate it. Use
  `git diff $(git merge-base main <branch>) <branch> -- <file>` to get only the agent's own
  changes, and re-verify previously merged work after each merge — not just the piece just landed.
- **Remove each worktree as it lands, not at the end.** Each is a full checkout; a wide wave can
  fill the disk mid-session, and worktree creation then fails with "No space left on device".
</system-reminder>

You have access to an `advisor` tool backed by a stronger reviewer model. It takes NO parameters -- when you call advisor(), your entire conversation history is automatically forwarded. They see the task, every tool call you've made, every result you've seen.

Call advisor BEFORE substantive work -- before writing, before committing to an interpretation, before building on an assumption. If the task requires orientation first (finding files, fetching a source, seeing what's there), do that, then call advisor. Orientation is not substantive work. Writing, editing, and declaring an answer are.

Also call advisor:
- When you believe the task is complete. BEFORE this call, make your deliverable durable: write the file, save the result, commit the change. The advisor call takes time; if the session ends during it, a durable result persists and an unwritten one doesn't.
- When stuck -- errors recurring, approach not converging, results that don't fit.
- When considering a change of approach.

On tasks longer than a few steps, call advisor at least once before committing to an approach and once before declaring done. On short reactive tasks where the next action is dictated by tool output you just read, you don't need to keep calling -- the advisor adds most of its value on the first call, before the approach crystallizes.

Give the advice serious weight. If you follow a step and it fails empirically, or you have primary-source evidence that contradicts a specific claim (the file says X, the paper states Y), adapt. A passing self-test is not evidence the advice is wrong -- it's evidence your test doesn't check what the advice is checking.

If you've already retrieved data pointing one way and the advisor points another: don't silently switch. Surface the conflict in one more advisor call -- "I found X, you suggest Y, which constraint breaks the tie?" The advisor saw your evidence but may have underweighted it; a reconcile call is cheaper than committing to the wrong branch.
</system-reminder>

- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

Based on my search results, I found relevant information about the Wulff et al. 2018 work on the description-experience gap.

Wulff et al. (2018) examined how people learn about probabilistic consequences in two ways: by consulting descriptions of an action's consequences and probabilities, or by personally experiencing the probabilistic consequences of an action.

The researchers reviewed potential determinants of the description-experience gap, finding that decision-makers may rely on small samples, weight recent observations more heavily (recency), or subjectively reverse probability weighting. However, there was no single determinant that could fully explain the gap.

Importantly, sampling error has been shown to be the primary source for the classic description-experience gap, with subjects showing a strong behavioral tendency to rely on small samples (insufficient information searches), which results in under- or non-observation of rare outcomes.

The Wulff et al. 2018 work was a meta-analysis that synthesized findings from multiple studies across different experimental paradigms to understand the systematic differences between description-based and experience-based decision-making.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding the Confidence Database and related research:

## The Confidence Database

The Confidence Database is a public resource that enables researchers to re-analyse a large corpus of studies into meta-cognitive confidence judgements.

## The Hard-Easy Effect and Overconfidence

The hard-easy effect is a common finding in confidence research, in which judges exhibit greater overconfidence for more difficult sets of questions. In signal detection studies, participants were asked to decide whether they heard a signal or noise and rate their certainty, with results confirming both overconfidence and the hard-easy effect.

## Explanations for the Hard-Easy Effect

The most parsimonious explanation for the hard-easy effect is that it is a regression-to-the-mean artifact, a byproduct of the noisy relationship between confidence and accuracy, since changes in difficulty have a more direct influence on accuracy than on confidence, and as task difficulty increases, performance drops, but if confidence is imperfectly responsive to this drop in accuracy, overconfidence must grow.

## Signal Detection and Noise

Novel frameworks can model confidence judgments in empirical datasets that may involve varying levels of task difficulty, and quantify metacognitive efficiency across difficulty levels. Additionally, model-based formulations of overconfidence can help bridge a gap between metacognition research and the literature on judgment and decision making.

## Overview

The hard–easy effect is a cognitive bias that manifests itself as a tendency to overestimate the probability of one's success at a task perceived as hard, and to underestimate the likelihood of one's success at a task perceived as easy.

## Manifestation in Metacognition

The hard-easy effect shows underconfidence (underestimation of correct rate) for easy or moderately difficult tasks and overconfidence (overestimation of correct rate) for very difficult tasks.

Item difficulty significantly impacts the accuracy and confidence level of individual judgments, leading to a "hard-easy effect" on the accuracy of confidence judgments, where individuals may display tendencies of overconfidence or a lack of confidence.

## Practical Examples

A consistent hard-easy effect emerged in a radiologic study: confidence was well-calibrated for easy cases but showed substantial overconfidence for difficult cases (>40%).

I found research related to your search query. Here are the key findings:

## CPC18 and Feedback Effects

The CPC18 design separates an initial no-feedback block from four subsequent blocks with outcome feedback, with the published prediction competitions treating the no-feedback block separately.

## BEAST's Performance with No Feedback

When researchers compared BEAST to classical decision models on decisions under risk without feedback (using only choices made without ambiguity in the first block of five trials), BEAST was expected to be at a significant disadvantage since its main assumptions concern the effects of feedback. However, BEAST was compared to Cumulative Prospect Theory, the Priority Heuristic, and the Decisions by Sampling model.

## Small Sample Analysis

Research examined the distribution of BEAST's Mean Squared Errors (MSEs) over 100 bootstrapped samples of size equal to the CPC 2018 training dataset (210 problems) versus performance on larger samples.

## BEAST and CPT Comparison

Organizers of CPC18 fitted and evaluated Cumulative Prospect Theory on the subset of data that includes only choice under risk without feedback, finding that its error is roughly twice that of BEAST.

The research demonstrates how feedback conditions affect prediction models' ability to forecast human decision-making in risky choice tasks.

https://openalex.org/W4313423775 2022 https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500009311 On the descriptive value of the reliance on small-samples assumption cit= 4
   ABS: Abstract Experience is the best teacher. Yet, in the context of repeated decisions, experience was found to trigger deviations from maximization in the direction of underweighting of rare events. Evaluations of alternative explanations for this bias led to contradicting conclusions. Studies that focused on the aggregate choice rates, including a series of choice prediction competitions, favored the assumption that this bias reflects reliance on small samples. In contrast, studies that focused on individual decisions suggest that the bias reflects a strong myopic tendency by a significant minority of participants. The current analysis clarifies the apparent inconsistency by reanalyzing a data set that previously led to contradicting conclusions. Our analysis suggests that the apparent inconsistency reflects the differing focus of the cognitive models. Specifically, sequential adjustment models (that assume sensitivity to the payoffs’ weighted averages) tend to find support for the hypothesis that the deviations from maximization are a product of strong positive recency (a form of myopia). Conversely, models assuming random sampling of past experiences tend to find support to the hypothesis that the deviations reflect reliance on small samples. We propose that the debate should be resolved by using the assumptions that provide better predictions. Applying this solution to the data set we analyzed shows that the random sampling assumption outperforms the weighted average assumption both when predicting the aggregate choice rates and when predicting the individual decisions.
https://openalex.org/W7124275542 2026 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2026.01.024 The robust beauty of small recent samples cit= 0
   ABS: 
https://openalex.org/W4415812160 2025 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2025.101769 How sampling strategies shape experience-based risky choice cit= 0
   ABS: Hallmark phenomena of risky choice, such as risk aversion and deviations from expected value (EV) maximization, are commonly modeled with psychoeconomic curves (e.g., utility function, probability weighting function). Yet these functions describe choices rather than the cognitive processes that generate them. Here, we examine how aspects of the oft-neglected process of information search - in particular, switching between options during sampling and stopping based on sampled evidence - can give rise to patterns in experience-based risky choice in the context of the sampling paradigm. We develop a computational framework that conceptualizes sampling strategies as consisting of three building blocks: a search rule (governing the rate of switching between options during sampling), a comparison rule (roundwise vs. summary evaluation of the options), and a stopping rule (decision threshold). In simulation analyses comparing different combinations of these building blocks, we show that frequent switching increases EV-maximizing choices for strategies with a summary comparison rule, but decreases maximization for strategies with a roundwise comparison rule. Further, frequent switching promotes an apparent underweighting of rarely experienced events found under the roundwise comparison rule, and curtails overweighting found under the summary comparison rule. We also reveal how the sampling strategies give rise to different risk attitudes depending on the existence and attractiveness of rare events. Finally, an empirical analysis suggests that people combine switching behavior and comparison rules in a way that fosters EV-maximizing choices. Our results underscore the possible contribution of search processes to patterns in risky choice.
https://openalex.org/W4392869450 2024 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2317751121 Frequent winners explain apparent skewness preferences in experience-based decisions cit= 10
   ABS: Do people's attitudes toward the (a)symmetry of an outcome distribution affect their choices? Financial investors seek return distributions with frequent small returns but few large ones, consistent with leading models of choice in economics and finance that assume right-skewed preferences. In contrast, many experiments in which decision-makers learn about choice options through experience find the opposite choice tendency, in favor of left-skewed options. To reconcile these seemingly contradicting findings, the present work investigates the effect of skewness on choices in experience-based decisions. Across seven studies, we show that apparent preferences for left-skewed outcome distributions are a consequence of those distributions having a higher value in most direct outcome comparisons, a "frequent-winner effect." By manipulating which option is the frequent winner, we show that choice tendencies for frequent winners can be obtained even with identical outcome distributions. Moreover, systematic choice tendencies in favor of right- or left-skewed options can be obtained by manipulating which option is experienced as the frequent winner. We also find evidence for an intrinsic preference for right-skewed outcome distributions. The frequent-winner phenomenon is robust to variations in outcome distributions and experimental paradigms. These findings are confirmed by computational analyses in which a reinforcement-learning model capturing frequent winning and intrinsic skewness preferences provides the best account of the data. Our work reconciles conflicting findings of aggregated behavior in financial markets and experiments and highlights the need for theories of decision-making sensitive to joint outcome distributions of the available options.
https://openalex.org/W3015295805 2022 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11166-022-09393-w An inquiry into the nature and causes of the Description - Experience gap cit= 11
   ABS: Abstract The Description-Experience gap (DE gap) is widely thought of as a tendency for people to act as if overweighting rare events when information about those events is derived from descriptions but as if underweighting rare events when they experience them through a sampling process. While there is now clear evidence that some form of DE gap exists, its causes, exact nature, and implications for decision theory remain unclear. We present a new experiment which examines in a unified design four distinct causal mechanisms that might drive the DE gap, attributing it respectively to information differences (sampling bias), to a feature of preferences (ambiguity sensitivity), or to aspects of cognition (likelihood representation and memory). Using a model-free approach, we elicit a DE gap similar in direction and size to the literature’s average and find that when each factor is considered in isolation, sampling bias stemming from under-represented rare events is the only significant driver of the gap. Yet, model-mediated analysis reveals the possibility of a smaller DE gap, existing even without information differences. Moreover, this form of analysis of our data indicates that even when information about them is obtained by sampling, rare events are generally overweighted.
https://openalex.org/W7123487863 2026 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67729-x Feedback-induced attitudinal changes in risk preferences cit= 0
   ABS: Decision-making under risk is often studied with fully described lotteries, where normative theory predicts that post-choice outcome disclosure (feedback) should not influence preferences. However, previous empirical work has generally shown that feedback does affect risk-taking, yet, without reaching a consensus on the consequences of feedback or the underlying cognitive mechanisms. Here, across seven behavioral experiments, we disentangle two competing accounts: the learning hypothesis, where feedback alters subjective values through experience, and the attitudinal hypothesis, where feedback changes preferences in anticipation of outcomes. We find that feedback does not improve maximization but consistently increases risk-taking. Fine-grained temporal analyses reveal that this effect emerges before any outcomes are experienced, ruling out learning as the primary driver. Moreover, the increase of risk-taking in partial feedback seems to be driven by curiosity, while in complete feedback by anticipated regret. Our results indicate that feedback can bias decision-making primarily through attitudinal rather than learning mechanisms.
https://openalex.org/W4409409462 2025 https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-025-00249-y Distributional dual-process model predicts strategic shifts in decision-making under uncertainty cit= 3
   ABS: In an uncertain world, human decision-making often involves adaptively leveraging different strategies to maximize gains. These strategic shifts, however, are overlooked by many traditional reinforcement learning models. Here, we incorporate parallel evaluation systems into distribution-based modeling and propose an entropy-weighted dual-process model that leverages Dirichlet and multivariate Gaussian distributions to represent frequency and value-based decision-making strategies, respectively. Model simulations and empirical tests demonstrated that our model outperformed traditional RL models by uniquely capturing participants' strategic change from value-based to frequency-based learning in response to heightened uncertainty. As reward variance increased, participants switched from focusing on actual rewards to using reward frequency as a proxy for value, thereby showing greater preference for more frequently rewarded but less valuable options. These findings suggest that increased uncertainty encourages the compensatory use of diverse evaluation methods, and our dual-process model provides a promising framework for studying multi-system decision-making in complex, multivariable contexts.
https://openalex.org/W4378800944 2023 https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009002042.007 The J/DM Separation Paradox and the Reliance on the Small Samples Hypothesis cit= 0
   ABS: Previous research demonstrates a large difference between decisions from description and decisions from experience, and also between decisions and probability judgment from experience. Comparison of decisions from description and from experience reveals a description–experience gap (Hertwig & Erev, 2009): higher sensitivity to rare events in decisions from description. Comparison of judgment and decisions from experience reveals the coexistence of overestimation and underweighting of rare events (Barron & Yechiam, 2009). The current review suggests that both sets of differences are examples of the J/DM separation paradox: While separated studies of judgment and decision making reveal oversensitivity to rare events, without the separation, these processes often lead to the opposite bias. Our analysis shows that the J/DM paradox can be the product of the fact that the separation of judgment from decisions making requires an explicit presentation of the rare events, and this mere presentation increases the apparent weighting of these events. In addition, our analysis suggests that feedback diminishes the mere presentation effect, but does not guarantee increase in rational behavior. When people can rely on accurate feedback, the main deviations from rational judgment and decision making can be captured with the reliance on the small samples hypothesis.
https://openalex.org/W4390789374 2024 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-023-01784-6 Modelling dataset bias in machine-learned theories of economic decision-making cit= 10
   ABS: Normative and descriptive models have long vied to explain and predict human risky choices, such as those between goods or gambles. A recent study reported the discovery of a new, more accurate model of human decision-making by training neural networks on a new online large-scale dataset, choices13k. Here we systematically analyse the relationships between several models and datasets using machine-learning methods and find evidence for dataset bias. Because participants' choices in stochastically dominated gambles were consistently skewed towards equipreference in the choices13k dataset, we hypothesized that this reflected increased decision noise. Indeed, a probabilistic generative model adding structured decision noise to a neural network trained on data from a laboratory study transferred best, that is, outperformed all models apart from those trained on choices13k. We conclude that a careful combination of theory and data analysis is still required to understand the complex interactions of machine-learning models and data of human risky choices.
https://openalex.org/W3003585144 2020 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-019-0813-1 The Confidence Database cit= 167
   ABS: Understanding how people rate their confidence is critical for the characterization of a wide range of perceptual, memory, motor and cognitive processes. To enable the continued exploration of these processes, we created a large database of confidence studies spanning a broad set of paradigms, participant populations and fields of study. The data from each study are structured in a common, easy-to-use format that can be easily imported and analysed using multiple software packages. Each dataset is accompanied by an explanation regarding the nature of the collected data. At the time of publication, the Confidence Database (which is available at https://osf.io/s46pr/) contained 145 datasets with data from more than 8,700 participants and almost 4 million trials. The database will remain open for new submissions indefinitely and is expected to continue to grow. Here we show the usefulness of this large collection of datasets in four different analyses that provide precise estimations of several foundational confidence-related effects.

# Paper Summary

**Title:** "How Many Mechanisms? Measuring Parsimony in Risky Choice"

**Author:** Avner Seror

**Abstract:** The research introduces a Maximum Rule Concentration Index to assess how efficiently risky choice datasets can be explained through simple decision rules from behavioral theories including salience, regret, disappointment, modal-payoff focusing, extreme-outcome screening, and limited attention. Applied to three lottery-choice datasets, the study finds that most subjects exhibit detectable parsimony—their choices concentrate around fewer mechanisms than standard utility models would predict, particularly organized around salience thinking, modal-payoff focusing, and regret.

**Data and Methods:** The provided content does not specify whether CPC15/CPC18 or choices13k datasets were used. There is no mention of model feedback blocks or small-sample models in the abstract or metadata presented.

Web search results for query: ""The robust beauty of small recent samples""

Links: [{"title":"The robust beauty of small recent samples - ScienceDirect","url":"https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0377221726000469"},{"title":"Small is beautiful: In defense of the small-N design","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6267527/"},{"title":"Robust Standard Errors in Small Samples: Some Practical Advice∗","url":"https://www.princeton.edu/~mkolesar/papers/small_robust.pdf"},{"title":"Robust estimation in very small samples - ScienceDirect","url":"https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167947302000786"},{"title":"(PDF) Robust estimation in very small samples","url":"https://www.researchgate.net/publication/223864903_Robust_estimation_in_very_small_samples"},{"title":"Robust estimation of risks from small samples - PMC","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5514355/"},{"title":"Small Samples, Big Insights: A Methodological Comparison of Estimation Techniques for Latent Divergent Thinking Models - PMC","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12653488/"},{"title":"Automating Ambiguity: Challenges and Pitfalls of Artificial Intelligence","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2206.04179"},{"title":"Robust Standard Errors in Small Samples: Some Practical Advice | The Review of Economics and Statistics | MIT Press","url":"https://direct.mit.edu/rest/article/98/4/701/58336/Robust-Standard-Errors-in-Small-Samples-Some"}]

Based on the search results, "The Robust Beauty of Small Recent Samples" is a research paper that draws on simulations, time-series analysis of managerial information environments, and an experiment.

The key findings of the research include:

The study shows that reliance on recent samples improves predictive accuracy in temporally dependent environments, that managerial environments are strongly temporally dependent, and that individuals adapt sample size to match environmental structure.

The paper challenges conventional organizational wisdom. While organizational theory typically advises managers to anticipate future conditions by gathering as much information as possible before making decisions, in practice people often rely on small samples of recent experience. The research concludes that it is good practice for managers to rely on small recent samples in prediction.

The research appears to be recent, with the ScienceDirect publication dated January 14, 2026.

https://openalex.org/W3163822076 2021 https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/buahk Examining the robustness of the relationship between metacognitive efficiency and metacognitive bias cit= 8
   ABS: We recently found a positive relationship between estimates of metacognitive efficiency and metacognitive bias. However, this relationship was only examined on a within-subject level and required binarizing the confidence scale, a technique that introduces methodological difficulties. Here we examined the robustness of the positive relationship between estimates of metacognitive efficiency and metacognitive bias by conducting two different types of analyses. First, we developed a new within-subject analysis technique where the original n-point confidence scale is transformed into two different (n-1)-point scales in a way that mimics a naturalistic change in confidence. Second, we examined the across-subject correlation between metacognitive efficiency and metacognitive bias. Importantly, for both types of analyses, we not only established the direction of the effect but also computed effect sizes. We applied both techniques to the data from three tasks from the Confidence Database (N > 400 in each). We found that both approaches revealed a small to medium positive relationship between metacognitive efficiency and metacognitive bias. These results demonstrate that the positive relationship between metacognitive efficiency and metacognitive bias is robust across several analysis techniques and datasets, and have important implications for future research.
https://openalex.org/W4295898232 2022 https://doi.org/10.7554/elife.75420 Reverse engineering of metacognition cit= 51
   ABS: The human ability to introspect on thoughts, perceptions or actions − metacognitive ability − has become a focal topic of both cognitive basic and clinical research. At the same time it has become increasingly clear that currently available quantitative tools are limited in their ability to make unconfounded inferences about metacognition. As a step forward, the present work introduces a comprehensive modeling framework of metacognition that allows for inferences about metacognitive noise and metacognitive biases during the readout of decision values or at the confidence reporting stage. The model assumes that confidence results from a continuous but noisy and potentially biased transformation of decision values, described by a confidence link function. A canonical set of metacognitive noise distributions is introduced which differ, amongst others, in their predictions about metacognitive sign flips of decision values. Successful recovery of model parameters is demonstrated, and the model is validated on an empirical data set. In particular, it is shown that metacognitive noise and bias parameters correlate with conventional behavioral measures. Crucially, in contrast to these conventional measures, metacognitive noise parameters inferred from the model are shown to be independent of performance. This work is accompanied by a toolbox ( ReMeta ) that allows researchers to estimate key parameters of metacognition in confidence datasets.
https://openalex.org/W4389725101 2023 https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001524 How do humans give confidence? A comprehensive comparison of process models of perceptual metacognition. cit= 48
   ABS: Humans have the metacognitive ability to assess the accuracy of their decisions via confidence judgments. Several computational models of confidence have been developed but not enough has been done to compare these models, making it difficult to adjudicate between them. Here, we compare 14 popular models of confidence that make various assumptions, such as confidence being derived from postdecisional evidence, from positive (decision-congruent) evidence, from posterior probability computations, or from a separate decision-making system for metacognitive judgments. We fit all models to three large experiments in which subjects completed a basic perceptual task with confidence ratings. In Experiments 1 and 2, the best-fitting model was the lognormal meta noise (LogN) model, which postulates that confidence is selectively corrupted by signal-dependent noise. However, in Experiment 3, the positive evidence (PE) model provided the best fits. We evaluated a new model combining the two consistently best-performing models-LogN and the weighted evidence and visibility (WEV). The resulting model, which we call logWEV, outperformed its individual counterparts and the PE model across all data sets, offering a better, more generalizable explanation for these data. Parameter and model recovery analyses showed mostly good recoverability but with important exceptions carrying implications for our ability to discriminate between models. Finally, we evaluated each model's ability to explain different patterns in the data, which led to additional insight into their performances. These results comprehensively characterize the relative adequacy of current confidence models to fit data from basic perceptual tasks and highlight the most plausible mechanisms underlying confidence gener
https://openalex.org/W4323265936 2023 https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/kdz34 Measures of metacognitive efficiency across cognitive models of decision confidence cit= 10
   ABS: Meta-d′/d′ has become the quasi-gold standard to quantify metacognitive efficiency because meta-d′/d′ was developed to control for discrimination performance, discrimination criteria, and confidence criteria even without the assumption of a specific generative model underlying confidence judgments. Using simulations, we demonstrate that meta-d′/d′ is not free from assumptions about confidence models: Only when we simulated data using a generative model of confidence according to which the evidence underlying confidence judgements is sampled independently from the evidence utilized in the choice process from a truncated Gaussian distribution, meta-d′/d′ was unaffected by discrimination performance, discrimination task criteria, and confidence criteria. According to five alternative generative models of confidence, there exist at least some combination of parameters where meta-d′/d′ is affected by discrimination performance, discrimination criteria and confidence criteria. A simulation using empirically fitted parameter sets showed that the magnitude of the correlation between meta-d′/d′ and discrimination performance, discrimination task criteria, and confidence criteria depends heavily on the generative model and the specific parameter set and varies between negligibly small and very large. These simulations imply that a difference in meta-d′/d′ between conditions does not necessarily reflect a difference in metacognitive efficiency but might as well be caused by a difference in discrimination performance, discrimination task criterion, or confidence criteria.
https://openalex.org/W4200446215 2021 https://doi.org/10.1101/2021.12.17.473249 Confidence as a noisy decision reliability estimate cit= 3
   ABS: Decisions vary in difficulty. Humans know this and typically report more confidence in easy than in difficult decisions. However, confidence reports do not perfectly track decision accuracy, but also reflect response biases and difficulty misjudgments. To isolate the quality of confidence reports, we developed a model of the decision-making process underlying choice-confidence data. In this model, confidence reflects a subject’s estimate of the reliability of their decision. The quality of this estimate is limited by the subject’s uncertainty about the uncertainty of the variable that informs their decision (“meta-uncertainty”). This model provides an accurate account of choice-confidence data across a broad range of perceptual and cognitive tasks, revealing that meta-uncertainty varies across subjects, is stable over time, generalizes across some domains, and can be manipulated experimentally. The model offers a parsimonious explanation for the computational processes that underlie and constrain the sense of confidence.
https://openalex.org/W4210904096 2022 https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-022-02063-7 Across-subject correlation between confidence and accuracy: A meta-analysis of the Confidence Database cit= 24
   ABS: 
https://openalex.org/W4386820332 2023 https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-022423-032425 Metacognition and Confidence: A Review and Synthesis cit= 252
   ABS: Determining the psychological, computational, and neural bases of confidence and uncertainty holds promise for understanding foundational aspects of human metacognition. While a neuroscience of confidence has focused on the mechanisms underpinning subpersonal phenomena such as representations of uncertainty in the visual or motor system, metacognition research has been concerned with personal-level beliefs and knowledge about self-performance. I provide a road map for bridging this divide by focusing on a particular class of confidence computation: propositional confidence in one's own (hypothetical) decisions or actions. Propositional confidence is informed by the observer's models of the world and their cognitive system, which may be more or less accurate-thus explaining why metacognitive judgments are inferential and sometimes diverge from task performance. Disparate findings on the neural basis of uncertainty and performance monitoring are integrated into a common framework, and a new understanding of the locus of action of metacognitive interventions is developed.

Based on the search results, I found the research you're looking for:

The paper "Bayesian inference with incomplete knowledge explains perceptual confidence and its deviations from accuracy" by Khalvati, Kiani, and Rao demonstrates that both choice and its associated confidence are explained by a Bayesian framework based on partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs).

The researchers tested their model on monkeys performing a direction-discrimination task with post-decision wagering, demonstrating that the model explains objective accuracy and predicts subjective confidence.

The model replicates well-known discrepancies of confidence and accuracy, including the hard-easy effect, opposing effects of stimulus volatility on confidence and accuracy, dependence of confidence ratings on simultaneous or sequential reports of choice and confidence, apparent difference between choice and confidence sensitivity, and seemingly disproportionate influence of choice-congruent evidence on confidence.

The paper was published in Nature Communications in September 2021 and represents a significant contribution to understanding how Bayesian inference with incomplete knowledge of the environment can explain both perceptual decision-making and the subjective confidence associated with those decisions.

## Key Findings

The hard-easy effect is a common finding in confidence research where judges exhibit greater overconfidence for more difficult sets of questions.

A Bayesian framework based on partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) replicates well-known discrepancies of confidence and accuracy, including the hard-easy effect, opposing effects of stimulus variability on confidence and accuracy, dependence of confidence ratings on simultaneous or sequential reports of choice and confidence, apparent difference between choice and confidence sensitivity, and seemingly disproportionate influence of choice-congruent evidence on confidence.

In perceptual judgments, subjects were underconfident when judgments were easy and overconfident when they were difficult.

Regarding explanations for the effect, many explanations have been advanced for the hard-easy effect, including systematic cognitive mechanisms, experimenter bias, random error, and statistical artifact, and necessary and sufficient conditions for observing a hard-easy effect can be mathematically derived.

The search results show that signal detection theory frameworks and Bayesian models have been used to explain how perceptual confidence and the hard-easy effect relate to noise and bias in decision-making tasks.

**Domain-Specific Patterns:**
Answers to questions involving general knowledge tend to produce overconfidence, whereas responses to perceptual tasks often result in underconfidence.

Using a transdiagnostic individual differences approach with a general population sample (N = 327), researchers quantified metacognitive patterns across memory and perception, finding that underconfidence was linked to anxiety-depression and overconfidence was linked to compulsivity.

**Calibration Analysis:**
Cognitive offloading impaired confidence calibration, with unaided decision makers showing the greatest alignment between confidence and accuracy. Additionally, offloading different cognitive processes produced distinct metacognitive biases: judgement offloading led to overconfidence, whereas combined offloading of memory and judgement processes led to underconfidence.

https://openalex.org/W2772751317 2017 https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000115 A meta-analytic review of two modes of learning and the description-experience gap. cit= 298
   ABS: People can learn about the probabilistic consequences of their actions in two ways: One is by consulting descriptions of an action's consequences and probabilities (e.g., reading up on a medication's side effects). The other is by personally experiencing the probabilistic consequences of an action (e.g., beta testing software). In principle, people taking each route can reach analogous states of knowledge and consequently make analogous decisions. In the last dozen years, however, research has demonstrated systematic discrepancies between description- and experienced-based choices. This description-experience gap has been attributed to factors including reliance on a small set of experience, the impact of recency, and different weighting of probability information in the two decision types. In this meta-analysis focusing on studies using the sampling paradigm of decisions from experience, we evaluated these and other determinants of the decision-experience gap by reference to more than 70,000 choices made by more than 6,000 participants. We found, first, a robust description-experience gap but also a key moderator, namely, problem structure. Second, the largest determinant of the gap was reliance on small samples and the associated sampling error: free to terminate search, individuals explored too little to experience all possible outcomes. Third, the gap persisted when sampling error was basically eliminated, suggesting other determinants. Fourth, the occurrence of recency was contingent on decision makers' autonomy to terminate search, consistent with the notion of optional stopping. Finally, we found indications of different probability weighting in decisions from experience versus decisions from description when the problem structure involved a risky and a safe option. (PsycINFO Database Record
https://openalex.org/W2013660131 2009 https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.683 A choice prediction competition: Choices from experience and from description cit= 346
   ABS: Abstract Erev, Ert, and Roth organized three choice prediction competitions focused on three related choice tasks: One shot decisions from description (decisions under risk), one shot decisions from experience, and repeated decisions from experience. Each competition was based on two experimental datasets: An estimation dataset, and a competition dataset. The studies that generated the two datasets used the same methods and subject pool, and examined decision problems randomly selected from the same distribution. After collecting the experimental data to be used for estimation, the organizers posted them on the Web, together with their fit with several baseline models, and challenged other researchers to compete to predict the results of the second (competition) set of experimental sessions. Fourteen teams responded to the challenge: The last seven authors of this paper are members of the winning teams. The results highlight the robustness of the difference between decisions from description and decisions from experience. The best predictions of decisions from descriptions were obtained with a stochastic variant of prospect theory assuming that the sensitivity to the weighted values decreases with the distance between the cumulative payoff functions. The best predictions of decisions from experience were obtained with models that assume reliance on small samples. Merits and limitations of the competition method are discussed.    ABS: ). Are there also discrepancies when people choose between a described and an experienced option? In two experiments, we compared people's behavior in a condition with mixed learning modes (i.e., one option described, the other experienced with the sampling paradigm) to that in conditions where both options were either described or experienced. Using cumulative prospect theory's value and probability weighting functions to characterize how observed outcome and probability information was subjectively distorted in people's choices, we found clear differences between the pure description and pure experience conditions. In the mixed-mode condition, however, the value and probability weighting functions did not differ between the described and the experienced options, suggesting that people evaluated them based on a joint representation despite the different learning modes. Participants' choices were not biased toward the described or the experienced option. Finally, per-option search effort for an experienced option tended to be higher in the mixed-mode condition than in the purely experience-based condition. Our findings demonstrate that how people evaluate described and experienced options depends on the learning mode of the other option in the choice set, highlighting a previously overlooked boundary condition of discrepancies between description- and experience-based choice.
