HAB22: Machine learning when theory fails
Although BEAST-GB achieved high accuracy in both CPC18 and Choices13k, these
successes may have arisen primarily because BEAST itself is already very effective for those
datasets. Indeed, in CPC18, the second-best submission was a minor modification of BEAST
(Table S1), and a scalable retrained variation of BEAST performed similarly to CD with
completeness of 88.3%.29 Furthermore, the original BEAST, without retraining of its
parameters, already captured much of the predictable variation in both CPC18 (88.9%
completeness) and Choices13k (65.7%). Thus, it remains unclear how much real benefit
comes from merging a strong behavioral model (BEAST) with ML, as opposed to simply
relying on the behavioral model alone.
To investigate this question, we turned to a dataset of risky-choice tasks recently
collected by He, Analytis, and Bhatia, henceforth, the HAB22 dataset.6 HAB22 differs from
CPC18 and Choices13k in several important ways (see Figure S3 and Table S5). First, it
includes data from multiple distinct experimental contexts. Second, it is restricted to choice
between lotteries with up to two outcomes and without feedback. Last, it includes data from
experiments designed to produce strong context effects.30 In many of the tasks from these
experiments, the lotteries’ EVs differed dramatically, and—potentially because of context
effects—participants often did not choose the option with the much higher EV.31,32 While
such tasks are useful for demonstrating interesting deviations from expected utility theory,
using them can hurt BEAST’s predictive power, as it assumes high sensitivity to EV
differences. Thus, HAB22 allowed us to examine the generality of our results in several
ways, as we show below.
Originally, HAB22 was used to evaluate 53 existing behavioral models by fitting
them to each participant’s data and then predicting the same individuals’ choices on new
tasks. BEAST-GB (like BEAST) was designed for predicting behavior of new decision
makers in new tasks, not for predicting known individuals. In the SI, we demonstrate that
models relying on BEAST-GB’s population-level predictions, together with BEAST’s
underlying logic, predict the individual choices in HAB22 as well as or better than the best

The work you're referring to appears to be "A Meta-Analytic Review of Two Modes of Learning and the Description–Experience Gap," by D. U. Wulff, M. Mergenthaler-Canseco, and R. Hertwig, published in 2018 in Psychological Bulletin.

**Research Focus:**

The research examined how people can learn about the probabilistic consequences of their actions in two ways: one by consulting descriptions of an action's consequences and probabilities (e.g., reading up on a medication's side effects), and the other by personally experiencing the probabilistic consequences of an action (e.g., beta testing software).

**Sampling Paradigm:**

The sampling paradigm consists of an initial sampling stage in which a person explores two payoff distributions without costs by clicking on one of two buttons on the computer screen. After completing sampling, the person sees a choice screen and is asked to make a final choice.

**Key Findings:**

A meta-analysis of more than 40,000 trials examining the average proportion of expected value-maximizing choices under description and experience found that the average gap size was about 20 percentage points when the choice problems included a risky option and a safe option.

The search results indicate this is a foundational meta-analytic study on how decisions based on descriptions versus personal experience differ systematically, with extensive analysis of the sampling paradigm used in such experimental designs.

I found several relevant results about the hot stove effect and Denrell's work. Here's what the search revealed:

## Overview of the Hot Stove Effect

The Hot Stove Effect suggests a sampling-based explanation of how biases in beliefs and attitudes can emerge from asymmetries in the information people get exposed to. The key mechanism is that people tend to avoid activities they have had a negative experience of, resulting in a negativity bias.

## Relationship to Risk Aversion

The hot stove effect implies a bias against a risky alternative in experience-based decisions, and the bias is a product of the tendency to reproduce actions that have been successful and avoid actions that led to loss. Errors of underestimation (an alternative is believed to be worse than it is) will be less likely to be corrected than errors of overestimation (an alternative is believed to be better than it is).

## Empirical Research on Small Samples

Previous research on experience-based decisions has led to mixed conclusions with regard to the descriptive value of the hot stove effect. Whereas some studies (e.g., Denrell & March, 2001) demonstrate its importance, other studies (e.g., Barron & Erev, 2003; Erev & Barron, 2005) suggest that this effect is weak. Research has examined this through experiments in which three choice problems were performed by the participants, each involving 400-fold binary choice between H (an alternative with higher expected value) and L (an alternative with lower expected value).

## Mitigation Through Feedback

The hot stove effect can be mitigated if individuals can learn not only from payoffs of the chosen option but also from the forgone outcomes of the unchosen alternative.

Here we show that, contrary to what is typically assumed, metacognitive inefficiency depends on the level of confidence. I found the research paper by Bourgin and Peterson! Based on the search results, here's what I found about their work on cognitive model priors:

The research focuses on decisions under risk (known payoff distributions) and under ambiguity (unknown probabilities), with and without feedback concerning the outcomes of past choices.

The researchers presented the first large-scale dataset for human decision-making, containing over 240,000 human judgments across over 13,000 decision problems. This is the "choices13k" dataset mentioned in your query.

They constructed "cognitive model priors" by pretraining neural networks with synthetic data generated by cognitive models (theoretical models developed by cognitive psychologists), and found that fine-tuning these networks on small datasets of real human decisions results in unprecedented state-of-the-art improvements on two benchmark datasets.

The feedback and no-feedback blocks were not required to be presented sequentially, and this alteration did not significantly affect overall predictive accuracy in their models, allowing them to more than halve the number of trials necessary.

The research was published in the Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2019) in June 2019.

Across-subject correlation between confidence and accuracy: A meta-analysis of the Confidence Database. Jin S, Verhaeghen P, Rahnev D. 2022
If one friend confidently tells us to buy Product A while another friend thinks that Product B is better but is not confident, we may go with the advice of our confident friend. Should we? The relationship between people's confidence and accuracy has been of great interest in many fields, especially in high-stakes situations like eyewitness testimony. However, there is still little consensus about how much we should trust someone's overall confidence level. Here, we examine the across-subject relationship between average accuracy and average confidence in 213 unique datasets from the Confidence Database. This approach allows us to empirically address this issue with unprecedented statistical power and check for the presence of various moderators. We find an across-subject correlation between average accuracy and average confidence of R = .22. Importantly, this relationship is much stronger for memory than for perception tasks ("domain effect"), as well as for confidence scales with fewer points ("granularity effect"). These results show that we should take one's confidence seriously (and perhaps buy Product A) and suggest several factors that moderate the relative consistency of how people make confidence judgments.

I did not change any files. Scratch outputs are in `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_novelty_EF_*.txt`. DOIs below come from OpenAlex, Crossref or Europe PMC, not from memory. Years are journal years; OpenAlex gives Wulff as 2017, the 2010 competition paper as 2009 and Shekhar & Rahnev as 2020.

## Candidate E: small-sample model predicting feedback shifts and the description–experience gap

**Closest modelling papers**
1. **BEAST, Erev et al. 2017 Psych Rev** (https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000062). BEAST assumes reliance on small samples. Its parameters were fitted on the CPC15 estimation set, and it then predicted choice rates per problem and per block ex ante: block 1 without feedback, blocks 2–5 with full feedback.
2. **Plonsky et al. 2025 Nat Hum Behav** (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02267-6; arXiv 1904.06866). BEAST with its original CPC15 parameters, not retrained, reaches 88.9% "completeness" on CPC18 and 65.7% on choices13k. The prediction targets are per-problem, per-block rates, so the feedback shift is predicted implicitly out of sample. BEAST-GB adds machine learning on top of BEAST.
3. **Peterson et al. 2021 Science and Bourgin et al. 2019 ICML (cognitive model priors).** choices13k has a `feedback` flag for each problem: block 1 has no feedback, blocks 2–5 have full feedback. Their neural networks therefore already model feedback versus no-feedback rates at scale. They are not small-sample models.
4. **Erev et al., description/experience choice prediction competition** (https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.683). The best out-of-sample predictions of per-problem experience-based choice came from small-sample models. Description was predicted by a separate prospect-theory variant. No single model with fixed parameters predicted both sides of the gap.
5. **Wulff, Mergenthaler-Canseco & Hertwig 2018** (https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000115). Reliance on small samples is named as the largest determinant of the gap, but this rests on moderator analyses. They did not fit a generative sampling model or predict the gap per problem.
6. **Related work:**
   - Plonsky, Teodorescu & Erev 2015 (https://doi.org/10.1037/a0039413).
   - "On the descriptive value of the reliance on small-samples assumption" 2022 (https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500009311): random-sampling models beat weighted-average models on one re-analysed dataset.
   - "The J/DM separation paradox…" 2023 (https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009002042.007): argues that feedback reduces the effect of merely presenting rare events.
   - I found no paper that fits a k-sample model to the Wulff database.

**Verdict: PARTLY DONE.**
- **CPC15/CPC18/choices13k side:** largely done. A small-sample model with frozen parameters (BEAST) already predicts per-problem feedback-block rates out of sample. What remains is:
  - showing that a minimal k-sample model (1–2 parameters) recovers most of this;
  - scoring the block-1-to-blocks-2–5 shift itself as the target, instead of block rates.

  This is a parsimony and decomposition result, not a first prediction.
- **Wulff-database side:** open. No one has used one fixed-parameter sampling model to predict the description–experience gap per problem across the database.

**Design constraints to flag**
- **No hot-stove test on CPC data.** CPC feedback blocks show forgone outcomes too. The hot-stove mechanism (avoided options never get re-sampled) cannot operate there. Only the small-sample part is testable.
- **Evidence against a pure learning account.** "Feedback-induced attitudinal changes in risk preferences" (Nat Commun 2026, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67729-x) reports, across seven experiments, that feedback raises risk-taking before any outcome is experienced. They attribute this to curiosity and anticipated regret, not learning. This works against a sampling account of the block-1-to-block-2 shift. Read it before committing to E.

**Confidence: medium.** The CPC side is verified from the primary text. That the Wulff side is open rests on the absence of hits in citation and web searches.

## Candidate F: hard–easy effect as a regression artefact in the Confidence Database

**Closest modelling papers**
1. **Guggenmos 2022 eLife, "Reverse engineering of metacognition"** (https://doi.org/10.7554/elife.75420). In simulation, a bias-free noisy observer shows apparent overconfidence that "increases as type 1 performance decreases, reminiscent of the classic hard-easy effect". The paper says the hard–easy effect "can be explained as a mere statistical artefact of random errors". Its model (ReMeta) was validated on one dataset only (Shekhar & Rahnev), not across the database.
2. **Merkle 2009 PBR, "The disutility of the hard-easy effect in choice confidence"** (https://doi.org/10.3758/pbr.16.1.204). Derives the conditions under which the effect appears from random error.
3. **Khalvati, Kiani & Rao 2021 Nat Commun** (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-25419-4). A Bayesian model reproduces the hard–easy effect, tested on monkey data.
4. **Ferrell 1995** (https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03206511) and **"Realism of confidence in sensory discrimination: the underconfidence phenomenon" 1993** (https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03206939). Earlier signal-detection noise models of perceptual calibration and underconfidence. Neither was applied to the Confidence Database.
5. **Confidence Database papers that are not about calibration:**
   - Jin, Verhaeghen & Rahnev 2022 PBR (https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-022-02063-7): across-subject correlation of confidence and accuracy (R = .22) in 213 datasets. This is not a within-dataset difficulty slope and was not modelled.
   - Xue, Shekhar & Rahnev 2021 (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/buahk): links metacognitive bias to metacognitive efficiency in 3 database tasks, not to fitted noise.
   - Rahnev et al. 2020 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-019-0813-1): its four example analyses cover confidence with choice and response time, serial dependence, and negative metacognitive sensitivity. None is about calibration.
   - Model-fitting work on database datasets is about metacognitive efficiency or model comparison, not the hard–easy effect:
     - Boundy-Singer, Ziemba & Goris 2023 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-022-01464-x);
     - Shekhar & Rahnev 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000249);
     - Guggenmos 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1093/nc/niab040);
     - Hellmann et al. 2023 (https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001524).

**Verdict: PARTLY DONE.**
- **Done:** the theory and simulation claim that a zero-bias noisy observer produces a hard–easy effect (Soll 1996, Merkle 2009, Guggenmos 2022, Khalvati 2021, plus Juslin et al. 2000 and Erev, Wallsten & Budescu 1994).
- **Not done:** fitting noise per dataset in the Confidence Database, predicting each dataset's hard–easy magnitude from that fit, and testing prediction against observation. I found no paper doing this.

**Design constraint:** calibration needs confidence on a probability scale, or an assumed mapping from ratings to probabilities. It also needs difficulty variation within a dataset. Many database datasets use 1–4 rating scales and a single difficulty level, so the usable subset may be small. This should be checked before committing to F.

**Confidence: medium.** A full-text search for "Confidence Database" plus "hard-easy" returned only ReMeta, and I checked its text directly. A recent preprint could still be missed.
